# Patent Family Tree: How to Read Patent Relationships


February 19, 2026


[Herbie Turner](https://www.linkedin.com/in/herbert-turner-1b511b238/)


Patent teams use a patent family tree to trace claimed priority, follow continuation branches, and identify records that need verification. The tree maps related applications, publications, and grants through reported priority, continuity, and national or regional phase relationships. Reading one accurately requires knowing which family definition the database uses, what each identifier represents, and which records support each link.


## Key takeaways


- A family tree indexes relationships and records. It does not prove priority entitlement, validity, status, ownership, or expiration.
- World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and European Patent Office (EPO) rules can produce different boundaries. Domestic, national, international, and foreign-oriented labels answer different questions.
- A Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) filing is an international application, not a worldwide patent.
- Read one relationship at a time. Confirm identifiers, links, dates, and source records.
- Office records, international databases, and an Application Data Sheet (ADS) can conflict. Investigate discrepancies.


## What a patent family tree shows


Most trees use **nodes** for applications, publications, or grants and **connections** for reported relationships. Those identifiers are related, but not interchangeable. Nodes may also show dates, jurisdiction, title, and status.


Connections can represent provisional benefit, a continuation, divisional, continuation-in-part (CIP), foreign priority, or a PCT phase entry. Position alone has no legal effect. Read the legend and relationship label.


*Screenshot of our patent-family visualization. The highlighted target is US 8,640,683, with parent US 8,371,282 above it. The graph helps locate records for review; it does not establish legal conclusions.*


This example shows US continuation, divisional, and CIP branches alongside PCT, European, and German records. A “tree” is often a graph because one record can connect to multiple earlier filings.


## Patent family types are different lenses


There is no single universal boundary around a patent family. The[EPO family definitions](https://www.epo.org/en/searching-for-patents/helpful-resources/first-time-here/patent-families) warn that databases can return different members because their definitions differ. The current[WIPO patent-family glossary](https://www.wipo.int/documents/d/standards/docs-en-08-01-01.pdf) defines several family types.


Family type Working definition What it helps answer


WIPO simple family Members share exactly the same originating application or set of applications as the basis of priority. Which publications share the same originating priority set?


EPO DOCDB simple family The EPO applies a simplified same-priority picture plus business rules. It considers first filings and US provisional first filings, treats US CIPs as equivalents to first filings, and places continuations and divisionals with the parent regardless of claimed priorities. Which records does the EPO treat as covering the same technical content?


Extended or INPADOC family Members are connected directly or indirectly through at least one shared priority. One member may bridge filings with different priority sets. What broader network of related filings may belong to the same development history?


National family Distinct related applications are published by the same office and share at least one originating application, as with continuations or divisionals. How did filing branch within one office?


Domestic family Different procedural publications from one office cover the same originating application. Which publications are stages of the same application?


International family A report-specific cross-jurisdiction metric. Some[WIPO landscape reports](https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/patent-landscape-report-agrifood/en/glossary.html) require publication in two or more jurisdictions. Which families meet the report's stated international-filing rule?


Foreign-oriented family[WIPO statistics](https://www.wipo.int/web-publications/world-intellectual-property-indicators-2025-highlights/en/patents-highlights.html) require at least one filing office outside the applicant's country of origin. A single filing can qualify when it was made only at a foreign office. Did the applicant file outside its home-country office?


These categories overlap, but international and foreign-oriented families are not synonyms. A US continuation chain may be both national and part of an INPADOC extended family. DOCDB has its own implemented rules, detailed in the[EPO's DOCDB guidance](https://www.epo.org/en/searching-for-patents/helpful-resources/first-time-here/patent-families/docdb) . Record the database and definition before comparing counts.


## How PCT applications and phase entries fit into the tree


A PCT application may claim earlier priority or be the first filing. It may enter selected national or regional phases, or have no phase entry. Patent grants remain under national or regional control, as the[USPTO's PCT overview](https://www.uspto.gov/patents/basics/international-protection/patent-cooperation-treaty) explains.


An international application may receive a WO publication number. The[PATENTSCOPE glossary](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/patentscope/db/glossary) defines the national phase as processing in the countries or regions where protection is sought.


A WO publication is not a worldwide grant, and designation does not show phase entry. Identify actual national or regional entries.


Use “U.S. national-stage application” only when the record confirms entry under 35 U.S.C. § 371. A U.S. application filed under § 111(a) as a continuation, divisional, or CIP of a PCT application is a bypass application, a distinct route explained in[MPEP § 1895](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s1895.html) and[§ 1896](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s1896.html) .


## How to read a patent family tree in six steps


### 1. Establish the tree's scope and legend


Identify the family definition, source, data date, and legend. Check whether the view includes unpublished applications, procedural publications, continuations, CIPs, PCT filings, and phase entries.


### 2. Separate application, publication, and patent numbers


Record the target's application, publication, and patent numbers. Normalize punctuation and country or kind codes without collapsing distinct records or confusing a provisional with a nonprovisional application.


### 3. Find the earliest claimed filing, then treat it as a lead


Trace the target backward through each labeled relationship. An early date is a claim or report, not a finding of entitlement. Current[MPEP § 211](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s211.html) separates the routes. For domestic benefit through prior nonprovisional or international applications under 35 U.S.C. §§ 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), identify each intermediate application and relationship and assess copendency. Provisional benefit under § 119(e) has separate timing and reference rules. Foreign priority under § 119(a) through (d), covered in[MPEP § 213](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s213.html) , is a distinct route.


### 4. Follow each branch one link at a time


For a continuation, divisional, or CIP, identify the immediate parent and filing date.[MPEP § 201.08](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s201.html) defines a CIP as adding matter not disclosed in the parent. Only adequately supported claims can receive the earlier date. Entitlement can require written-description and enablement support under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), alongside route-specific requirements.


### 5. Trace PCT records into actual jurisdictions


Locate the international application and WO publication, then list the national or regional phase entries shown. Keep the international filing date, any claimed priority date, and each phase event distinct. In the United States, confirm whether the record is a § 371 national-stage application or a § 111(a) bypass application.


### 6. Open the underlying records


Use the graph to select file wrappers, ADS versions, specifications, priority documents, legal-event registers, and assignment records for review. The source documents support the answers.


## What a family tree can and cannot support


### Validity and priority analysis


A tree can locate candidate priority chains, provisionals, CIPs, and possible gaps. It can also frame a date window for searching intervening prior art. It cannot establish that a claim receives an earlier date. That analysis can require route-specific priority or benefit requirements and claim-specific written-description and enablement support under § 112(a).


### Prosecution and claim evolution


Branches identify which prosecution histories and claims to compare. Continuations and divisionals show where scope moved, while a CIP calls for separating old and added disclosure. File wrappers and claim text supply the substance. See our guide to[prosecution history analysis](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/how-and-ai-transforms-prosecution-history-analysis) .


### Portfolio analysis


A family view can reveal filing breadth, concentration by jurisdiction, pending branches, and records that merit status review. It cannot prove ownership, enforceability, remaining term, or expiration. Assignments, maintenance events, terminal disclaimers, term adjustments or extensions, and jurisdiction-specific registers require separate analysis.


The boundary is firm: a graph helps identify records and issues. It does not prove priority entitlement, validity, legal status, ownership, or expiration. Underlying records and claim-specific support require attorney review.


## Why patent family data is imperfect


Family relationships are distributed across office data, filing documents, international databases, and later corrections. Sources update at different times and normalize identifiers differently. A link can appear in one record and be absent from another. A number can be transposed, a date can reflect the wrong event, or a database can use a different family definition.


The ADS is useful and important to verify. Current[MPEP § 601.05](https://www.uspto.gov/web/offices/pac/mpep/s601.html) defines it as bibliographic data and describes corrected ADS treatment. The USPTO's[ADS completion instructions](https://www.uspto.gov/patents/apply/forms/important-information-completing-application-data-sheet-ads) warn that benefit claims must be ordered correctly and explain how corrections are marked.


Three discrepancy categories catch many practical problems:


- **Relationship existence in either source:** a parent-child relationship appears in the ADS but not Patent Center, or in Patent Center but not the ADS.
- **Relationship type:** the sources show the same parent-child pair but disagree on continuation, divisional, CIP, § 371 national stage, or another link.
- **Filing date:** the sources associate the same application with different filing dates.


*ADS excerpt illustrating a detected discrepancy. The screenshot lists 61/976,445, while the[child's published specification](https://patents.google.com/patent/US20200066107A1/en) identifies 61/976,554. The system records one missing relationship and one extra relationship rather than creating a separate application-number discrepancy.*


Because a relationship is matched by its parent and child application numbers, a wrong or transposed number creates paired missing-and-extra existence records. The system detects and preserves both records without changing the graph or deciding what the priority record should be. Corrected ADSs, filing receipts, the file history, the provisional record, and claim-specific support provide the evidence needed to investigate the difference.


## How &AI builds and reconciles the graph


&AI constructs the graph recursively from a target application. We query Patent Center continuity data for direct relationships, add newly discovered applications as nodes, and repeat until no unseen connected applications remain within the chosen sources and family scope. If Patent Center has no continuity data, the ADS builds the graph.


We assemble relationships from multiple sources. Structured US records can describe domestic continuity, international sources can expose cross-jurisdiction records, and the ADS can show what the applicant submitted. The reconciliation process retains these source-specific inputs for comparison.


Our reconciliation layer checks the ADS against the assembled graph using the three discrepancy categories above. The child ADS selects an active relationship type only when the assembled records contain more than one type for the same parent-child pair. A direct disagreement between Patent Center and the ADS about relationship type is detected and preserved for review without changing the graph. Existence mismatches are likewise detected and preserved for review without graph changes. Filing-date mismatches are detected and logged for investigation. The same source-grounded approach supports our broader work on[patent document parsing](https://www.tryandai.com/blog/how-and-ai-solved-patent-parsing) .


## Patent family verification checklist


Before relying on a family tree for legal or business analysis:


- Record the database, family definition, query date, and tree legend.
- Match application, publication, and patent numbers to the correct records.
- Confirm each direct continuity or priority link in the underlying office record and filing documents.
- Review the current and corrected ADS versions, filing receipts, and specifications.
- Separate PCT international-phase records from actual national or regional phase entries.
- Check status in the relevant office register as of the date that matters.
- Review assignment and ownership records separately.
- Calculate term and expiration separately, including adjustments, extensions, disclaimers, and maintenance events where relevant.
- Test priority claim by claim against the applicable route and § 112(a) support with counsel.
- Preserve discrepancies and source provenance in the work product.


## Frequently asked questions


### What is the difference between a patent family and a patent family tree?


A patent family is a group of related patent records under a stated definition. A patent family tree is the visual representation of those records and their reported priority, continuity, or national or regional phase relationships.


### Does the earliest date in a patent family tree establish priority?


No. It identifies an early claimed or reported filing date. Priority entitlement can depend on the specific claim, the accuracy and timing of benefit claims, the continuity chain, and support in the earlier application.


### What is the difference between a simple and extended patent family?


A WIPO simple family groups members with the same originating application or set. An extended family connects records that share at least one priority directly or through another member. The EPO's DOCDB family uses a simplified priority picture plus business-rule exceptions, so it should not be treated as identical to WIPO's definition.


### Does a PCT application create a worldwide patent?


No. A PCT filing begins an international application process. Patent grants remain with national or regional offices. The applicant may pursue selected phase entries, but a PCT filing does not show that any phase entry occurred.


### Can a patent family tree show whether a patent has expired?


A tree may display a status label, but it does not prove expiration or enforceability. Confirm the office register and analyze term, fees, adjustments, extensions, disclaimers, and relevant legal events separately.
